claims.text: The last open question in multi-shop-requirements.md asks what level of service shops are promised in the contract, to be answered before the first shop signs.
An SLO is a target for one SLI over a time window, such as 99.5% of order requests not answered with a 5xx over a rolling 28 days (glossary; outline item 1).
slo.md uses one window for all SLOs: a rolling 28 days, chosen so that every window has the same number of weekend days.
SLO targets in slo.md: S1 99.5% (shops can sell; SLA below), S2 99% and S3 99.5% (source CH-3), S4 99% (source YC-7). S2 = order POSTs answered within le=0.512; S3 = product GETs without 5xx.

slo.md: no SLO is 100%; the API depends on PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ and Keycloak, each fails at times, so 100% cannot be met and forbids every risky change, bug-fix releases included. Policy: allowance used up -> feature releases stop until the SLI is back above the SLO.

SLA to shops (assumed, pending contract), for S1 only: 99% of order requests without error per calendar month; a month below gives the shop a service credit against the next period; set below the SLO on purpose.
0.5% of 28 days (40,320 minutes) is 201.6 minutes, about 3 hours 22 minutes; 1% of a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) is 432 minutes, 7 hours 12 minutes.
In the lab, slo-report.sh reads a 1-hour window instead of 28 days.
YC-7: a customer's refund request is received and answered within 2 seconds, even when the payment gateway does not answer or reports an error; it states no percentage.
CH-3: a shop's busy day does not slow the other shops; YC-9: an order is never refunded twice. Opinion: when a need must hold for every request, it belongs in the design and its tests, not in an SLO.
A target should come from a written need rather than today's measured ratio; today's ratio may serve as a first guess only when no need is written down yet, and should be replaced once one is.

slo.md sets the SLA below the SLO on purpose, so that when S1 drops under 99.5% the team should see it while there is room before the contract is broken; equal numbers mean the first miss already breaks the contract.

If a shop asks for an SLA above the SLO (e.g. 99.9%), do not sign under the current SLO; raise the SLO first, only if the team can keep it. If needs are unchanged, do not raise the SLO just because the measured ratio is higher.

A rolling window can be read on any day and keeps one bad day in view for four weeks; a calendar month matches how the SLA in slo.md and its credits are counted, starts again on the first, and months differ in length.

beyond_scope: Calendar month vs rolling window as a trade-off row (claim 14), to explain why SLO and SLA use different windows as slo.md shows.
YC-9 named as a need that belongs in the design and its tests, not an SLO (one sentence under Trade-offs).
